steps.explanationAfterStep: The protonated ester is delocalised over both oxygens and its carbonyl carbon is far more electrophilic.
The hydroxyl oxygen reaches the carbonyl carbon from above the plane of the C=O, at the Bürgi–Dunitz angle: 5-exo-trig, favoured by Baldwin's rules. The breaking C=O π bond lies outside the new ring.
A fast proton transfer gives the neutral tetrahedral intermediate.
Protonation turns methoxide, a poor leaving group, into methanol, a good one.
The lone pair on the OH oxygen pushes out methanol and becomes the C=O π bond again.
The acid is returned, so only a catalytic amount is needed. Five-membered lactones form so readily that γ-hydroxy acids and esters often close on standing.

title: Lactonisation of a γ-hydroxy ester
subtitle: An intramolecular transesterification closes a five-membered ring: 5-exo-trig at C=O
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 31 (Saturated heterocycles and stereoelectronics)
Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 10 (Nucleophilic substitution at the carbonyl group)

reactants.caption: methyl 4-hydroxybutanoate + sulfuric acid (catalytic)
hintTiers: An ester carbonyl is a weak electrophile. How does acid make it a better one?
The carbonyl oxygen takes a proton from sulfuric acid; the O–H bonding pair stays on the acid's oxygen. Two arrows.
Carbonyl oxygen lone pair → new O–H bond to the acidic hydrogen; that O–H bond → lone pair on the acid's oxygen.
reactants.learnerPrompt: A hydroxy ester in acid. First, activate the ester.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The neutral ester carbonyl is a poor electrophile for a neutral alcohol. Protonate the carbonyl oxygen first.
The carbonyl oxygen is the more basic oxygen of an ester: its protonated form is delocalised. Protonate the C=O.
Protonating the OH group helps nothing: the hydroxyl must stay a nucleophile. Activate the ester carbonyl.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the carbonyl oxygen takes the proton. Where does the O–H bonding pair go?

tetrahedral.caption: neutral tetrahedral intermediate + sulfuric acid
hintTiers: Which group should leave to give the lactone, and how does acid make it leave as a neutral molecule?
The methoxy oxygen takes a proton from sulfuric acid. Two arrows.
Methoxy oxygen lone pair → new O–H bond to the acid's hydrogen; that O–H bond → lone pair on the acid's oxygen.
tetrahedral.learnerPrompt: Make the methoxy group into a leaving group.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Protonating the ring oxygen leads back to the open chain. To make the lactone, methanol must leave.
If water left, the product would be a cyclic oxocarbenium ion, not the lactone. Methanol is the group to lose.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right oxygen. Where does the O–H bonding pair of the acid go?

ring-oxonium.caption: cyclic tetrahedral intermediate, protonated on the ring oxygen
hintTiers: Which oxygen is the most basic site here, and which species is the acid?
Hydrogen sulfate takes the proton from the positively charged ring oxygen. Two arrows.
Hydrogen sulfate oxygen lone pair → new O–H bond to the ring oxygen's hydrogen; that O–H bond → lone pair on the ring oxygen.
ring-oxonium.learnerPrompt: Remove the extra proton from the ring oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Breaking the new ring bond is the way back. Remove the proton from the ring oxygen instead.
Methoxide is a poor leaving group. First move a proton so that methanol, a neutral molecule, can leave.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: hydrogen sulfate takes that proton. Where does the O–H bonding pair go?

protonated-ester.caption: protonated ester + hydrogen sulfate
hintTiers: Count along the chain: which ring size forms if the hydroxyl oxygen reaches the carbonyl carbon?
The hydroxyl oxygen bonds to the carbonyl carbon, and the C=O π pair moves onto the protonated oxygen. A five-membered ring forms. Two arrows.
Hydroxyl oxygen lone pair → new O–C bond to the carbonyl carbon; C=O π bond → lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.
protonated-ester.learnerPrompt: The hydroxyl group at the end of the chain attacks. Close the ring.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: That gives the proton back and undoes the activation. The hydroxyl oxygen can now attack.
That carbon is not electrophilic. The protonated carbonyl carbon is.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: the ring is closing. The carbonyl carbon has five bonds: move the C=O π pair.

protonated-lactone.caption: protonated lactone + methanol
hintTiers: Which oxygen is the most basic site here, and which species is the acid?
Hydrogen sulfate takes the proton from the protonated carbonyl oxygen. Two arrows.
Hydrogen sulfate oxygen lone pair → new O–H bond to that hydrogen; that O–H bond → lone pair on the carbonyl oxygen.
protonated-lactone.learnerPrompt: Return the proton to the acid.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Methanol adding back reverses the last step. Removing the proton finishes the lactone; excess methanol is distilled off.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right. Where does the O–H bonding pair go?

protonated-methoxy.caption: tetrahedral intermediate with a protonated methoxy group
hintTiers: A lone pair on a neighbouring oxygen can push the leaving group out. Which oxygen will become the C=O?
The OH oxygen forms a C=O π bond as the C–O bond to the protonated methoxy group breaks. Two arrows.
OH oxygen lone pair → π bond to the ring carbon; C–O bond to the methoxy oxygen → lone pair on that oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The ring oxygen could push methanol out too, giving a cyclic cation without C=O. The OH oxygen gives the protonated lactone directly.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: methanol leaves. Carbon now has only three bonds: which lone pair fills the gap?

mechanismSummary: Acid protonates the ester carbonyl, and the hydroxyl group at the other end of the chain adds to it, closing a five-membered ring. Proton transfers turn the methoxy group into methanol, which leaves as the OH oxygen re-forms the C=O; loss of the proton gives γ-butyrolactone. The ring closure is 5-exo-trig: the nucleophile reaches the trigonal carbonyl carbon at the Bürgi–Dunitz angle from outside the ring. Five-membered lactones form so easily that γ-hydroxy acids often cyclise on their own.
